You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: 
- What the failing test asserts:
  - ArchiveStreamFactoryTest.testEncodingInputStream iterates over predefined test cases. For each, it:
    - Creates an ArchiveInputStream via factory.createArchiveInputStream(type, inputStream).
    - Reflectively reads a specific field from the created stream (using getField(instance, fieldName)).
    - Compares that value to the expected encoding string from the test data.
  - If the stream didn’t receive the factory’s encoding, the reflected field will not match the expected value and the test counts a failure.

- Reported symptom:
  - The issue report states that ArchiveStreamFactory fails to pass on the encoding when creating these streams: ArjArchiveInputStream, CpioArchiveInputStream, DumpArchiveInputStream, JarArchiveInputStream, and JarArchiveOutputStream.

- Relevant implementation observations:
  - ArchiveStreamFactory has an “encoding” refactor that introduced two fields: encoding and entryEncoding. The constructor ArchiveStreamFactory(String encoding) assigns both fields:
    - this.encoding = encoding;
    - this.entryEncoding = encoding;  // comment: keep using the original field
  - In createArchiveInputStream(String, InputStream), the factory checks entryEncoding when deciding whether to call a two-arg constructor:
    - For ARJ, CPIO, DUMP, JAR (as well as ZIP and TAR), the code uses:
      - if (entryEncoding != null) new XArchiveInputStream(in, entryEncoding) else new XArchiveInputStream(in).
  - This means the propagation of the encoding depends on entryEncoding being set.

- How the failure happens:
  - After the refactor that introduced an additional “encoding” field (to address immutability/thread-safety concerns), not all code paths keep entryEncoding and encoding in sync anymore. For example, if the factory’s encoding is set via a path that updates only encoding (and not entryEncoding), entryEncoding remains null.
  - In createArchiveInputStream, the decision to pass the encoding into the stream constructors is based solely on entryEncoding. If entryEncoding is null, the factory will use the single-argument constructors for ARJ, CPIO, DUMP, and JAR — i.e., it won’t pass the encoding at all — even though encoding itself may have been configured.
  - Consequently, for those formats, the created streams’ internal encoding-related field remains unset or defaulted, which the test detects via reflection; the observed field value doesn’t match the expected encoding string, and the test fails.
  - The issue report also mentions JarArchiveOutputStream; the same pattern applies on the output side: the factory method for creating output streams likewise fails to pass the configured encoding in at least the JAR case due to relying on the wrong field or not passing the argument at all.

- Why only some formats show up in the report:
  - The propagation logic is inconsistent across formats and factory methods. Some formats may incidentally get the encoding because the relevant code path uses a field that was kept in sync, or because the tests set encoding via the constructor (which assigns both fields), while others are affected when encoding is configured via a path that only updates encoding but not entryEncoding.

In short, the factory’s create methods look at entryEncoding to decide whether to pass an encoding to constructors, but after the refactor, encoding and entryEncoding can diverge. When entryEncoding is null, the factory creates ARJ/CPIO/DUMP/JAR streams without passing the encoding, causing the test’s reflective checks to see a mismatch with the expected encoding.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
